blocks.value:
# Four questions before the first line of code

A six-person team spent five months building a bank reconciliation module for an ERP. It came out pretty, fast, fully tested. Six weeks after launch, 31 clients had opened the screen and 4 had come back a second time. Nobody got the code wrong. The team erred earlier: it built the right thing that almost nobody wanted that way.

Marty Cagan describes four risks every product carries that need answers BEFORE building, not after. VALUE risk: do people want this enough to abandon their current way? USABILITY risk: can they use it without someone explaining over their shoulder? TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY risk: can it be built with the team, deadline, and data that exist today? BUSINESS FEASIBILITY risk: does it fit the commercial model, legal, support cost, and brand?

Notice only the third is about code, and it is precisely the only one most teams check before starting. The other three bring products down just as easily and are usually answered by guesswork in a meeting nobody recorded. Discovery is the work of answering these four questions spending days, not quarters.

[["Risk","The question it asks","Who pulls the answer"],["Value","Do people want it and will they switch?","PM, with user evidence"],["Usability","Can they use it without help?","Design, with a task test"],["Technical feasibility","Can we build and sustain it?","Engineering, with a short investigation"],["Business feasibility","Does it fit cost, legal, and brand?","PM with the involved areas"]]
The risk that brings down the most products is not the technical one. It is value: impeccable code perfectly solving a problem nobody had.

## Who answers, and why together

Each risk has a natural owner, but none resolves itself alone. Whoever leads the answer on value is usually the PM, closest to user and business; usability is design's territory; technical feasibility is engineering's; business feasibility is the PM's with legal, finance, support, and sales at the table.

The detail that changes the outcome is the TRIO: PM, design, and engineering doing discovery together, in the same conversation, hearing the same user. When the PM interviews alone and later retells the story, much of the information evaporates on the way, and the team that will build receives conclusion instead of evidence. When engineering hears the pain straight from the source, the cheap solution nobody had imagined appears; when design hears, the flow detail that did not fit the summary appears.

The anti-pattern is the delivery team: the requirement arrives ready, the team estimates, builds, and launches. The four risks were answered by opinion in some meeting, and the bill only appears when the number does not move. Discovery inverts that: the team joins the question, not just the answer.

lessons.title: The cost of building the wrong thing

blocks.value:
# The five-month treadmill bill

Let us put a number on the pain. A six-person team costs, with charges and overhead, somewhere between 120 and 180 thousand reais a month across much of the Brazilian market. Five months of treadmill dedicated to a module nobody uses are six hundred thousand reais or more that became screen.

But the bill does not stop there, and the invisible part is usually bigger than the visible one. There is the OPPORTUNITY COST: in those five months, the team did not attack the problem that was truly bleeding, and the competitor did. There is the MAINTENANCE COST: code nobody uses keeps being migrated, tested, updated for security, and considered in every refactoring for years. There is the COMPLEXITY COST: every dead function takes space in the menu, the documentation, support training, and the head of whoever arrives new.

And there is the quietest cost of all, team morale. After the second launch that dies without use, people stop asking why and start delivering cards. The team becomes a factory that does not believe in its own product.

[["Where the error appears","Cost to fix","What was already spent"],["In the interview","One sentence and one new question","Half an hour of conversation"],["In the prototype","Redoing three screens","Two days of design"],["In code review","Reviewing the implementation","Weeks of building"],["In production","Fixing, migrating, communicating","Whole cycle plus support"],["Never fixed","Living with the dead function","Years of maintenance"]]
The company's most expensive code is not the badly written one. It is the one that should never have been written and now must be maintained forever.

## Discovery as cheap insurance

Compare the bill with the price of the insurance. Eight forty-minute interviews with the trio cost two afternoons of three people. A clickable prototype tested with five users costs about two days. A demand test with one page and one button costs less than a week. That whole package stays well below five percent of the quarter's budget, and it exists to answer the question deciding the other ninety-five percent.

The rule worth carrying: the later the error is discovered, the more expensive it gets, and the curve is not gentle. An assumption knocked down in a conversation costs embarrassment. The same assumption knocked down after launch costs the whole cycle, plus client communication, plus data migration, plus time nobody recovers.

Discovery is no guarantee of being right, and promising that is dishonest. It is risk reduction: you trade the chance of losing five months for the certainty of losing two weeks finding out. Mature teams do not do discovery to be right; they do it to discover early, and cheaply, when they are wrong.

lessons.title: Continuous discovery vs the research project

blocks.value:
# Research that arrives late decides nothing

The script is well known. The company hires a market study, the agency goes to the field for three months, delivers an eighty-page document with colorful personas and a one-hour presentation. Everyone praises it. Two weeks later, the file is in a folder nobody opens, and the team keeps deciding the same way as before: by the hunch of whoever is most convincing in the meeting.

The problem is not the study's quality. It is the RHYTHM mismatch. The team makes dozens of small decisions a week, and the study arrives once a semester, answering questions that already changed. Worse: because it cost a lot and took long, the study becomes sacred truth for a year, even when the market moved.

Teresa Torres calls the alternative continuous discovery: at least one user contact per week, made by the trio that builds, tied to a specific outcome. It is not the same work compressed; it is different work. The big study produces knowledge; continuous discovery produces DECISIONS, in the week the decision needs to be made.

[["Aspect","Research project","Continuous discovery"],["Rhythm","Once a semester","Every week, nonstop"],["Who does it","Agency or specialist only","The trio that will build"],["Deliverable","Report and presentation","The week's decision and test"],["Recruiting","Task force per round","A pipe kept on all the time"],["Validity","Ages fast in the drawer","Corrected by the next round"]]
Research that becomes a report informs. Research that becomes a weekly habit changes what the team builds on Monday morning.

THE TRIO'S WEEK (continuous discovery)

Monday, 30 minutes
  Review the quarter's outcome.
  Pick the week's question (just one).

Tuesday and Wednesday
  2 interviews of 30 to 45 minutes.
  PM leads, design takes literal notes, engineering watches quietly.
  Automatic in-product invite for whoever did the target action in the last 7 days.

Thursday, 60 minutes
  Synthesis together: excerpts become cards, cards become opportunities.
  Update the opportunity tree.

Friday, 30 minutes
  Pick the riskiest assumption and design next week's test.
  Record the decision taken and what knocked it down or supported it.

## What changes when it becomes routine

Notice what the agenda above solves without heroic effort. Recruiting stops being a project and becomes a running pipe: the invite goes out automatically to whoever did the action of interest, and there are always people in the queue. Synthesis happens with the conversation fresh, not three weeks later. And the trio decides together, which eliminates the step of convincing the team of something it did not hear.

Two interviews a week look like little, and that is where the beauty lies: that is about one hundred contacts a year, more than any big study delivers, spread over time instead of concentrated in one month. Every week the team corrects the course a little, and a course error corrected early costs almost nothing.

This does not eliminate the big study. Entering a new market, changing positioning, and heavy investment decisions need depth a weekly conversation cannot give. The practical rule is simple: big research for the big, rare decision; continuous discovery for the dozens of small decisions that, added up, define the product.

lessons.title: Double diamond with a critical reading

blocks.value:
# Two diamonds, four movements

The double diamond is the most reproduced drawing in product design: two lozenges side by side, each with a part that opens and a part that closes. In the first diamond you work the PROBLEM. In the discover phase, you open: interview, observe, gather signal from every side, without falling in love with any explanation. In the define phase, you close: group, choose, and write which problem is worth attacking.

The second diamond works the SOLUTION. In develop, you open again: generate many ideas, prototype, test alternatives competing with each other. In deliver, you close: pick one, refine, and ship.

The central idea is that each movement has its own mental posture, and mixing the two destroys both. Whoever judges while diverging kills the strange idea that would have been the good one. Whoever diverges when they should converge never decides anything and the project becomes an endless talking circle. Saying out loud 'we are opening now, nobody criticizes yet' solves half of product's unproductive meetings, and that may be the drawing's greatest practical value.

[["Phase","Movement","Central question","Typical output"],["Discover","Opens","What is going on?","Raw opportunities"],["Define","Closes","Which problem to attack?","The chosen problem"],["Develop","Opens","In how many ways could we?","Tested alternatives"],["Deliver","Closes","What ships, and how?","Solution live"]]
The double diamond is a great vocabulary and a terrible schedule. It serves to say where you are, not to promise when you finish.

## Good as a map, dangerous as a process

Now the critical reading, which almost never accompanies the drawing. In practice, nobody walks the two diamonds once and in a straight line. You enter the develop phase, test a prototype, and discover you understood the wrong problem; you go back to the first diamond. That is not an execution failure, it is the normal functioning of work with uncertainty. But the drawing, with those arrows always pointing forward, suggests otherwise.

From that comes the most common distortion: the double diamond becoming a waterfall with a nice name. It shows up as a project phase on the schedule, with eight weeks of discovery before any user conversation, a report delivered at the end of each lozenge, and a baton pass to the next team. When there is a handoff between diamonds, the team that builds receives a ready conclusion and loses the context only gained by listening.

The healthy use is far more modest. Use it as shared vocabulary to ask 'are we opening or closing right now?', and accept that the cycle is short and repeats. A diamond that lasts two weeks teaches more than one that lasts two quarters.

# Not all evidence weighs the same

Two sentences arrive at the same meeting. The first: 'I talked with four clients and they all found the idea excellent'. The second: 'three clients signed letters of intent with value'. Both are evidence. But one cost the speaker nothing, and the other cost reputation and money. Confusing the two is like accepting a promise and a receipt at the same value.

It is worth carrying a mental ladder. On the lowest rung is OPINION about the future: finding it pretty, saying you would use it, praising the idea. Next comes AGGREGATED USAGE DATA: the dashboard showing 78 percent stop at the document step, strong for saying where it hurts, mute about why. Above that, the STATEMENT about past fact: 'last week I exported three times and checked by hand', which already has context and is hard to invent. Higher up, OBSERVED BEHAVIOR: you watched the person try and get stuck. At the top, COMMITMENT: money, signature, time given, sensitive data handed over.

The ladder is not rigid, and the point is not ranking for sport. It is asking, before deciding, which rung what supports the decision came from.

[["Level","Typical example","Answers well","Where it deceives"],["Opinion","Loved the idea","Almost nothing","Courtesy becomes false signal"],["Usage data","78 percent abandon there","Where and how much","Silent about why"],["Statement","I did that three times this week","Past context","Selective memory"],["Observed","Watched the person get stuck","What actually happens","Artificial setting"],["Commitment","Paid, signed, gave time","Intensity of desire","Small, expensive sample"]]
Praise is kindness, sign-up is interest, a credit card is evidence. Charge each decision the rung it deserves.

## How to climb the ladder without spending much

Climbing is usually cheaper than it looks. If you received a compliment, ask for the fact: 'when was the last time you needed this?'. If you received a strong statement, ask to see: 'show me how you do it today'. If observed behavior confirmed the pain, charge a small commitment: joining a list, giving thirty minutes a week in the pilot, referring a colleague, paying a symbolic amount. Each rung costs one more question, and is worth far more than repeating the previous rung.

Two cautions. The first is proportional decisions: climbing to the top of the ladder to pick a button's color is waste, and deciding the quarter's bet on hallway opinion is reckless. Ask for strong evidence where the decision is expensive and irreversible.

The second is honesty when reporting. When presenting the result, say which rung each piece came from: 'six people stated, two we watched doing, none paid anything yet'. A sentence like that is worth more than any chart, because it puts everyone in front of the same degree of uncertainty.

blocks.value:
# Whom you invite decides what you learn

You want to test an idea for an app managing a sales team's expenses. You message your eight closest contacts, everyone replies within an hour, everyone finds it brilliant. Three months later the product is live and nobody activates. The problem was not how the conversations were run: it was the guest list.

A discovery interview serves to hear whoever HAS the problem, not whoever likes you. Three profiles are gold. The CURRENT USER shows where the product gets stuck in real use. The USER WHO CHURNED is the most uncomfortable and most informative: they tried, gave up, and know exactly where it hurt. And the NON-USER of the target segment, the one who has the problem and solves it another way, reveals the real competitor, which is almost always a spreadsheet, WhatsApp, or a patient intern.

Two guests poison the sample. The team's friend wants to help you and will agree with everything you say. And whoever shows up attracted by a high incentive answers to get the prize, not to solve their life.

[["Whom you invite","What it usually reveals","Risk of hearing only that"],["Current user","Where use gets stuck today","Only improves what exists"],["Who churned","The real reason for giving up","Hard to find and schedule"],["Non-user in the segment","How they solve without you","May not have the problem at all"],["Team friend","Praise and goodwill","Agrees with everything you say"],["Attracted by a big prize","The fastest path to the gift","Invents problems they do not have"]]

## How many, and where they come from

The practical rule: 5 to 8 people per segment per round. From the fifth or sixth conversation onward, within the same profile, patterns start repeating, which is what research calls SATURATION: the tenth interview costs the same as the first and brings almost no new information. If answers still surprise you by the eighth, you probably mixed two different segments in one list.

The channels that work, from cheapest to most expensive: the product's own base, filtering by behavior in the database (whoever used the report three times last month, whoever stopped logging in in May); the waitlist; support, which knows by heart who complained about what; the client community; and, last, paid recruiting with an external panel.

All of them include a short SCREENING questionnaire, the screener. And it asks about behavior, never intention. None of 'would you be interested in better controlling the team's expenses?'. Ask 'how many times did you report expenses in the last 30 days?' and 'which tool did you use last time?'. Everyone declares interest; behavior separates whoever lives the problem from whoever just finds the topic nice.
Interviewing people who like you is group therapy. Research is interviewing whoever has the problem, including whoever already gave up on you.

## Recruiting is a running pipe, not a task force

Teresa Torres calls CONTINUOUS DISCOVERY the habit of talking with a user every week, and its bottleneck is almost never the conversation: it is finding people. Teams that treat recruiting as a project ('next week we organize the interviews') spend half the month scheduling. Teams that treat it as a pipe keep the flow on: an in-product invite for whoever just used the feature, an automatic scheduling link, two fixed slots per week the team commits to filling.

The incentive enters proportionally to the effort: a voucher, a gift, plan credit, a donation in the person's name. Too high and you buy the interviewee, who becomes a research professional and pretends to have any problem you describe.

And there is a trap no incentive solves: SURVIVORSHIP BIAS. Whoever answers your invite is whoever still uses and still likes it. Whoever canceled does not answer, does not open the email, and may not even be in your base anymore. If the whole round comes from whoever stayed, the conclusion always sounds too good. It is worth paying the price of hunting two or three churners per round, even if each costs five attempts.

lessons.title: Asking about life, not about the idea

blocks.value:
# The forbidden question is 'would you use it?'

You present the idea in a twenty-minute call, show three screens, and ask: 'would you use this?'. The person smiles and says yes, that it would be sorely missed, that it is exactly what the market needs. You repeat with seven more, and all seven say the same. You launch, and the page converts four sign-ups in two weeks.

Nobody lied to you. People are polite and optimistic: praising costs zero, and imagining yourself organized in the future is a pleasant fantasy. 'Would you use it?' asks for an OPINION ABOUT THE FUTURE, and opinion about the future is the weakest rung of the evidence ladder. What you want is PAST FACT: what the person did, when they did it, with which tool, how much it cost, and what happened afterwards.

The swap is easy to state and hard to sustain in the heat of conversation, because the idea is yours and you want to talk about it. As long as the question points to the future and to your solution, the answer will be courtesy. When it points to the past and to the person's life, it becomes data.

## The mom test, in plain words

Rob Fitzpatrick proposed a simple filter for your questions and named it the mom test. The idea: your mom loves you, wants to see you happy, and will praise anything you invent. A good question is one even she cannot answer with empty praise, because it asks for no opinion at all, it asks for fact.

'Mom, would you use an app to organize the family recipes?' is far from passing: the answer is 'of course, dear'. Now try this: 'tell me about the last time you looked for an old recipe. Where was it? How long did it take to find? What did you do when you could not?'. There is no escape through praise; either she remembers the episode, or she admits it does not happen.

Notice what changed: your idea vanished from the sentence. You did not ask for evaluation, you asked for story. Questions that survive the test almost always look the same: what did you DO, WHEN was the last time, HOW MUCH did you spend, WHAT did you use, HOW did that end. If your question can be answered with 'that would be great', it is not ready to leave the house.

[["Bad question","Good question","What the good one reveals"],["Would you pay 30 reais a month?","How much have you already spent on this this year?","Priority measured in money"],["Does this screen look good?","Show me how you did it last time","The real path and shortcuts"],["Would you use an app for this?","When was the last time it hurt?","Pain frequency and severity"],["Is this a problem for you?","What have you already tried to solve it?","Effort invested in the topic"],["Would you like a report?","Who demands this number, and when?","Who really runs the flow"]]
Praise is social noise and comes free. Time, reputation, and money cost dearly: that is why only they count as signal.

## Praise is noise, commitment is signal

After each conversation, separate what the person SAID from what they DID. 'Loved it, it is very good' does not go in the report: it is kindness. 'I built a spreadsheet on Sunday to close this' does, because it is observed behavior, with date and effort.

The next level is commitment, and it has several currencies besides money. The person sending you their real spreadsheet, with their data, is commitment. Accepting a second 40-minute conversation next week is commitment. Introducing you to the manager who approves the purchase is expensive commitment, because they put their reputation on it. Signing a pre-order or paying upfront is the strongest signal there is, and that is exactly why it is rare.

When praise appears mid-interview, and it will, do not fight the person. Use it as a hook to a fact: 'glad it makes sense, tell me about the last time this got in your way'. Either you find the real episode behind the praise, or you discover there was no episode at all. Both answers are useful; only the first becomes product.

blocks.value:
# A compass, not a track

Two interviews with the same script. In the first, the person starts telling how she rebuilds the hospital shift schedule every Sunday night, and the interviewer cuts in: 'cool, but back to question 4...'. In the second, the interviewer leaves the script for ten minutes, follows the story, and discovers the schedule is redone because the system does not warn when one doctor swaps with a colleague. Question 4 would never have gotten there.

The script exists so you do not forget what needs covering and so two of the team's interviews are comparable later. It does not exist to be read in order, word for word. Whoever reads the script aloud runs a spoken form, and people answer forms on autopilot.

The session lasts 30 to 45 minutes. Less than that leaves no time to get past the rehearsed answer; more than that and the person tires and starts answering to wrap up. Within that window, the goal is not covering the twelve questions: it is leaving with two or three SPECIFIC STORIES, with a date, a tool name, and what happened afterwards.

## The anatomy of the conversation

The OPENING takes about three minutes and does more work than it seems: who you are, why you invited that person, how long it will take, a request to record, and two sentences that loosen the interviewee, said in full words: there is no wrong answer here, and I did not come to sell you anything.

Then comes the WARM-UP about the routine: what your day is like, who you work with, what passes through your hands. It serves to calibrate your vocabulary and for the person to hear themselves talking.

The heart is the SPECIFIC STORY: 'tell me about the last time you had to redo a shift schedule'. Notice the difference from 'how do you usually do it?'. The generic question returns an idealized process, the one the person thinks they follow; 'the last time' returns memory, with the improvisation, the 11 p.m. WhatsApp, and the parallel spreadsheet.

From the episode onward it is DEEPENING: so what did you do next, how long did it take, who else got involved, why that way. And the CLOSING: what should I have asked and did not, who else lives this, may I reach out again.

INTERVIEW SCRIPT (35 to 45 min)
Product: hospital shift schedule management
Profile: nursing coordinator who builds the schedule

1. OPENING (3 min)
   I am Joao, from the product team.
   I did not come to sell anything, I came to understand how you build schedules today.
   There is no wrong answer; what gets in your way is what interests me.
   May I record just so nothing is lost? It stays with the team.

2. WARM-UP (5 min)
   What is a normal day like for you in coordination?
   How many people are on the schedule you manage?
   Who depends on that schedule once it is ready?

3. SPECIFIC STORY (15 min)
   Tell me about the last time you had to redo a schedule.
   When was that? Which day, what time?
   What happened before? How did you find out?
   What did you use to solve it? Show me on screen, if you can.

4. DEEPEN (10 min)
   So what did you do next?
   How long did it take from start to finish?
   Who else had to step in to solve it?
   Why that way, and not another?
   What have you tried before that did not work?

5. CLOSING (4 min)
   What should I have asked and did not?
   Who else lives this and would talk to me?
   May I reach out if a question comes up? Thanks for the time.

# Three seconds of silence are worth a question

The person answers, pauses, and the anxious interviewer follows with the next question right away. The best part of the interview is lost right there. A pause is not embarrassment: it is the person finishing remembering. Count to three in silence after they stop talking, looking like you are still listening, and most of the time they complete it themselves: 'oh, and there was that time I had to call the on-call doctor at eleven at night'.

SILENCE is the cheapest tool you have and the hardest to use, because instinct says fill the void. The other vices are relatives of the same instinct to occupy space: finishing the other person's sentence, correcting them when they use the wrong name for a function, stacking two questions in one ('and how was that, did you find it hard?'), and answering for them when they take long.

Each of these takes the conversation out of the interviewee's head and into yours. You leave the call with answers, but they are your answers spoken with another person's voice. It is the worst kind of data: looks like research and is echo.

[["Interviewer vice","What it causes","Instead"],["Following a question into the pause","Loses the complement","Count to three in silence"],["Explaining the solution mid-way","It becomes a demo, and it is over","Return to the problem"],["Is it not frustrating when it freezes?","Plants the emotion in the person","How was it last time?"],["Two questions in one","They answer only one","One at a time, and wait"],["Correcting their term","They start policing themselves","Write down their word"]]
The minute you start explaining your solution, the interview is over and has become a demo. Nobody tells you, though.

## Write down the sentence, not your conclusion

The interviewee says: 'I redo the schedule on Sunday night because I only find out about the swap when somebody does not show up'. You write: 'user wants swap notification'. Done, the data died. What is left is your solution hypothesis, and it can no longer be reviewed, because the original sentence exists nowhere.

Write it LITERALLY, in quotes, with the person's vocabulary. If they call it a 'broken schedule', write broken schedule, not 'allocation inconsistency'. The raw sentence survives changes of opinion: three weeks from now, when the team debates whether the problem is the notification or the swap process, the quote decides. Today's interpretation only repeats what you already thought before entering the call.

Interpreting has its moment, and the moment is afterwards. During the conversation, your job is capturing: what they did, in which words they told it, which number came up. In doubt between writing fast and understanding well, write fast. That is exactly why there is a second person in the room.

## Roles, recording, and the care not to intimidate

A good interview has two separate roles. Whoever LEADS looks at the person, asks one question at a time, and watches the pace. Whoever TAKES NOTES stays quiet, records literal quotes with the timestamp, and only enters at the end with the questions left dangling. Doing both alone is possible, but you will lose half the lines or half the eye contact.

Record, always with explicit consent said out loud at the start: what it is for, who will see it, how long it is kept. The recording frees the interviewer from transcription and allows checking the exact quote later.

Watch the ratio: three people from the team against one interviewee is not an interview, it is an examining board. The person becomes a student in an oral exam and starts giving the answer they think is right. Two on your side is the ceiling.

And when they ask for the solution ('and will you build a button for this?'), promise nothing and do not debate the button. Log it as a request, thank them, and return to the problem: 'I wrote it down. And today, when this happens, what do you do?'.

# An interview without synthesis becomes a memory

Friday, the team closed nine interviews that week. The recordings are in the folder, the notes in three different documents, everybody's head full of good stories. Two weeks later, in the prioritization meeting, someone asks what the research showed, and out comes: 'there was this guy who said something really interesting about a report'. Nine conversations became one anecdote.

SYNTHESIS is the step that turns conversation into team knowledge, and it has a deadline: 24 to 48 hours after the interview, while memory still holds the context the notes did not capture. Past that, you depend on the pure transcript and the cost triples.

And it is done together, by the TRIO: PM, design, and engineering. Not because it looks nice in the process, but because each one hears something different. Design notices the hesitation on the screen, engineering notices that number comes from a system nobody integrates, the PM notices the effect on the contract. Synthesis done by one person alone produces what that person already thought before, now with a supporting quote.

## From raw to insight, in four steps

The path is always the same, and each step loses volume and gains meaning. First, the RAW: recording, transcript, notes. Second, the EXCERPTS: you sweep the material and cut only what is observed behavior or strong speech, always in the person's words. 'I redo the schedule on Sunday night' is an excerpt; 'dissatisfied user' is not.

Third, the CARDS: each excerpt becomes a card with the quote, who said it, and the context. Fourth, grouping by similarity, the AFFINITY MAP: you spread the cards, join the ones talking about the same thing, and let the group form itself, with no category decided beforehand. A group too big is usually vague; a group with a single card is not yet a pattern, it is a case.

Each stable group becomes a named OPPORTUNITY, and the name comes from the user's language, not your internal vocabulary. 'Finding out about the shift swap too late' is an opportunity name. 'Notifications module' is a solution name, and it is not solutions you are mapping at this step.

[["What came up in the conversation","How to classify","What to do with it"],["I redo the schedule every Sunday","Pain, with behavior","Becomes a strong opportunity"],["I wish I could see it all in one place","Stated desire","Store it and look for evidence"],["Put an export button there","Requested solution","Ask about the problem behind"],["I spent 400 reais on a spreadsheet","Pain, with money","The round's strongest signal"]]
Counting how many people asked for the same feature is not research, it is a ballot. Research is discovering what they tried before asking.

## What makes an insight actionable

An insight that serves decisions has four parts: WHO (the segment, not 'the users'), IN WHAT SITUATION (the trigger, the moment), WHAT THEY TRIED (today's homemade solution), and WHAT GOT STUCK (where the attempt fails). Miss one of these and the team goes back to debating opinion.

Compare. Useless version: 'coordinators want more notifications'. Actionable version: 'a nursing coordinator at a mid-size hospital, when an on-call doctor swaps with a colleague without warning, finds out via WhatsApp the day before and redoes the schedule by hand on Sunday night, because the system only shows the published schedule'. The second can be measured, can be designed on top of, and can be challenged with data.

Always separate PAIN, DESIRE, and REQUESTED SOLUTION. Pain has behavioral evidence; desire is what the person would like; a requested solution is what they told you to build, and it is the most dangerous, because it arrives ready and saves you your thinking.

With a pile of well-named opportunities in hand, the next question is inevitable: which of them connect, and where to start. That is where the list needs to become a map.

# A tree in place of the list

At the quarter review, a director asks why the team is building the internal chat. The answer comes out rambling: 'it was in the backlog', 'the big client asked', 'every competitor has it'. Nobody can show the path leaving the business goal and arriving at that screen. It is not the team's bad faith: the prioritized list simply stores that path nowhere.

The OPPORTUNITY SOLUTION TREE, proposed by Teresa Torres, is the drawing that stores it. At the top sits an OUTCOME, a measurable behavior result like 'increase the 30-day repeat purchase rate'. On the next level come the OPPORTUNITIES: pains, needs, and desires that appeared in interviews, grouped into branches and sub-branches. At the leaves sit the SOLUTIONS, what the team can build. Below each solution sit the ASSUMPTION TESTS, which say whether it holds before becoming a quarter of work.

Read bottom up, the tree answers the director without improvisation: this chat attacks the opportunity of not knowing whether the order will be late, which appeared in six of nine interviews, and that opportunity is one of the paths to the quarter's outcome. Read top down, it shows what could also have been done and was not.

OST OF A USED-FURNITURE MARKETPLACE

OUTCOME: increase the 30-day repeat purchase rate
  OPPORTUNITY: I do not trust the furniture's real condition
    sub: the listing photo hides the defect
      SOLUTION: mandatory four-angle photo
        TEST: 20 new listings with the mandatory flow
      SOLUTION: badge for sellers who accept returns
        TEST: offer the badge in 3 categories
    sub: I do not know whether the seller replies
  OPPORTUNITY: the delivery price catches me by surprise
  OPPORTUNITY: I bought once and forgot it exists
A prioritized backlog says what comes first. The tree says why that is on the list, and what you chose not to do.

## Why the tree disciplines

Three things change when the drawing exists. First: it becomes visible that the fashionable solution serves ONE branch among many. The chat solves a piece of waiting anxiety and does not touch the other two branches that appeared in the same interviews. Without the tree, that cut is invisible and the team thinks it is attacking the whole problem.

Second: the tree forces comparison before commitment. Closing a quarter on one branch means giving up the others for three months, and that trade deserves to be made with the branches side by side, not in the impulse of the meeting where someone spoke loudest.

Third: 'why are we doing this?' gets a drawn answer instead of an excuse invented later. Notice the prioritized backlog list does none of this. It stores the delivery order and throws away the reasoning that produced it. Six weeks later, nobody remembers whether that item entered because the evidence was strong or because there was space left in the sprint. The tree stores both ends: what the team decided to do and what it decided to leave for later.

# The button hiding a pain

An ERP client opens a short ticket: 'I need an export-to-Excel button'. The team logs it, estimates, delivers. Three weeks later the same client complains again, now about something else. The button was never the subject.

Behind the request there was an opportunity: 'I need to show my boss the week's number and I do not trust what the screen shows'. Notice the distance between the two sentences. The button is ONE possible solution for that pain, and not even the best: if the problem is trust in the number, exporting to Excel only moves the distrust somewhere else.

That is discovery's most common confusion. People do not describe pains, they describe solutions, because that is how we speak day to day. Nobody asks for 'I need certainty about the weekly closing'; they ask for a button, an integration, a screen. Every requested solution hides an opportunity, and translating one into the other is the work.

Translating uses three simple questions: what would you do with it once you had it, when did you last need it, and how did you solve it without. The three pull story, and story is where the real pain appears.

TRANSLATING A REQUEST INTO AN OPPORTUNITY

Raw request: 'I want an export-to-Excel button'

1. What would you do with the file after downloading?
   'I put together the week's summary for my manager'
2. When was the last time you needed this?
   'last Friday, spent two hours checking'
3. How did you solve it without the button?
   'typed into a spreadsheet and checked item by item'

Opportunity: I need to close the week's number
              and trust it
Possible solutions: closing dashboard,
                    discrepancy alert,
                    cross-check between two reports

[["Raw request","Opportunity behind it","Possible solutions"],["ERP: export to Excel","Close the week's number with trust","Weekly dashboard, discrepancy alert"],["Delivery: chat with the courier","Know whether the order will be late","Live tracking, delay notice"],["HR: free field in reviews","Record what was agreed without embarrassment","Private note, conversation script"],["Billing: boleto on WhatsApp","Be warned before the boleto is due","Reminder on the channel the person uses"]]
Every feature request is an answer. Discovery's work is discovering what the question was.

## How to recognize a well-written opportunity

A good opportunity has four marks. It is in the USER'S VOICE, with the words they used in the interview. It is in the present tense, because it is something that already happens to them, not something that would happen if the product existed. It embeds no technology: it describes the pain, never the mechanism. And it is specific enough to fit a test, meaning you can imagine how we would know if it disappeared.

Three formats usually disguise themselves as opportunities and are not. The vague one: 'improve the experience' says nothing about what hurts, for whom, or when. The one disguised as a solution: 'have WhatsApp integration' has already chosen the path and closes the range before the conversation starts. And the business goal: 'increase revenue' is the company's result, nobody's pain; it can even be the top outcome, but it is never an opportunity.

It is worth insisting on a point that looks like detail: translating WIDENS the range instead of closing it. When the request becomes 'I need to close the week's number and trust it', paths nobody had considered appear, from the closing dashboard to the alert warning when two reports disagree. With the button on the table, the conversation was already over.

# A living tree, not a kickoff slide

The team does an offsite, draws a beautiful OST, takes a screenshot, and posts it on the wiki. Three months later, fifteen new interviews became fifteen separate documents nobody opens, and the tree in the screenshot stays exactly the same. It became decoration.

The tree is a LIVING artifact of the trio (PM, design, and engineering), updated at the same rhythm as continuous discovery. Each weekly interview round produces new opportunities, and each of them does one of two things: fits a branch that already exists, and confidence in that branch rises (the fourth person saying the same thing is worth much more than the first), or fits nowhere, and opens a new branch that was outside your map.

Usage data feeds the tree from another side, and it is important not to confuse the two roles. A funnel plunging from 100 to 40 at a sign-up step points to WHERE to look for an opportunity. It does not say WHICH pain it is: it may be confusion, distrust, or a document the person does not have on hand at that moment. The number picks the conversation's place; the conversation discovers the content.

A tree only one person touches becomes that person's opinion with a nice drawing around it.

## Hygiene, home, and ritual

A living artifact gathers dirt. Duplicates are the most common: 'I do not know whether it arrived' and 'I wonder whether the boleto registered' are the same opportunity in different words, and must become one, summing both pieces of evidence. A branch nobody touched in three months deserves review: either the pain vanished, or you stopped asking about it. And each opportunity keeps the link to the interview excerpt that originated it, with person, date, and minute. That traceability is what lets you answer 'where did you get this?' without resorting to memory.

Two mistakes bring the practice down. The first is leaving the tree with one person only: it becomes their opinion, and the team does not even disagree, because it did not join the building. The second is treating each interview as an independent document; with no shared place, last week's learning does not talk to this week's.

In 2026, the tree's home is usually a shared board tool, a category that exists in any company. Do not look for the perfect product. Look for the place the trio opens every week, and set aside thirty fixed minutes on the calendar to update the drawing together.

# Where to bet the quarter

The tree has four branches and everyone wants to attack all four. It cannot be done: the quarter is finite and the team is the same. Then what always happens happens, and you have seen it: the branch of the client who shouted loudest at renewal gets picked, or the branch the executive mentioned in the hallway. In both cases the decision was made, just without a criterion anyone can repeat later.

Choosing a branch with explicit criteria costs one hour and saves months. There are five questions. PAIN SIZE: how severe is it when it happens? REACH: how many people in the segment live this? FREQUENCY: does it happen once a year or every Friday? ALIGNMENT: does solving it move the top outcome? If not, it is a legitimate opportunity, but for another tree. CAPACITY: can we attack this in the coming months, with the team we have?

One detail changes the outcome: the comparison is between SIBLING BRANCHES, those on the same level disputing the same outcome. Comparing a huge opportunity with a tiny sub-branch of another family is the fastest way to arrive at a number that means nothing.

Choosing a branch is choosing what not to do. If the decision does not hurt a little, you chose nothing.

## The decision must be written

In the table above, the data-trust branch wins comfortably. The tie between the other two is the interesting moment: surprise delivery hurts more, forgetting reaches more people, and the tiebreak criterion is alignment with the outcome. If the outcome speaks of repeat purchase in 30 days, the forgetting branch sits closer to it. The score does not decide alone; it organizes the conversation and shows where people disagree.

Once the choice is made, record it. Three lines suffice: which branch we chose, why it, what stayed out and why. Keep it next to the tree, with a date. In six weeks someone will ask 'why did we not do that other one?', and the difference between a ten-second answer and an hour of re-discussion is exactly this record existing.

Watch for the anti-pattern. When the choice comes from the client who shouted loudest or the executive who commanded, the request is still evidence: it enters the count as one more signal, weighed by the same criteria as the others. What must not happen is the voice's volume replacing the whole comparison.

# The first idea is the obvious one

Branch chosen, someone says 'so it is a weekly dashboard' and the whole room agrees in four seconds. It looks like efficiency. It is the cheapest way to lose a quarter: the first idea is almost always the most obvious one, already circling everyone's head, and marrying it dispenses exactly the comparison that would let you discover something better.

The antidote is volume before filter. For the chosen branch, generate 10 to 15 ideas. Start ALONE, in silence, each person writing their own list: if the session starts open, everyone anchors on the first idea said out loud, usually by the person with the longest tenure. Only afterwards read everything together, one idea at a time, without debating yet.

Include quotas forcing the team off the obvious: two ideas with no technology at all (a phone call, a manual brigade, an arrangement with the operations team) and two intentionally absurd ideas. The absurd ones rarely become product, but almost always reveal the hidden assumption inside the serious ideas, and that is what you want to see now, not three months from now.

IDEATION SESSION FOR THE 'I DO NOT TRUST THE NUMBER' BRANCH (60 MIN)

00:00 Reread the opportunity and two interview excerpts
00:10 Alone, in silence: 10 ideas each, no filter
00:25 Reading round, one idea at a time, no debate
00:40 Check the mandatory quotas:
        two ideas with no technology at all
        two intentionally absurd ideas
        two ideas another company would do better
00:50 Group the similar ones and keep 3 competitors

[["Candidate","Moves the outcome?","Effort","Most fragile assumption"],["Closing dashboard","High","Medium","The person opens the dashboard on Friday"],["Discrepancy alert","Medium","Low","We can detect the discrepancy"],["Human-assisted closing","High","High","Operations handles the volume"]]
A single solution on the table is not a choice, it is a prophecy: the team will find reasons for it to work.

## Three competitors, not one favorite

After volume comes the cut. Filter down to THREE solutions attacking the SAME opportunity by different paths, because only then does real comparison exist. A lone solution becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy: the team investigates it lovingly, finds reasons for it to work, and calls that validation. Ten solutions do not work either, for a very prosaic reason: investigating properly costs time, and you do not have time for ten.

Compare the three by three lenses. Potential to move the outcome: if it works, how much does the behavior up top change? Perceived effort: an order of magnitude combined with engineering, no false-precision estimate. And fragile-assumption dependence: how much each path leans on something we believe but have never seen happen.

The third lens usually changes the order. The most exciting solution is sometimes the one leaning on the largest number of 'if people do X'. Notice none of the three is approved for passing this comparison. Each carries assumptions that still need to be listed, prioritized, and tested, and that is what separates a conscious bet from a well-presented guess.

# Every solution is a stack of bets

A clinic's product trio decides to build an app for patients to reschedule appointments on their own. It looks obvious, everyone agrees, it enters the roadmap. Underneath that decision is a stack of bets nobody wrote: that the patient prefers the app to calling the front desk, that they find the button without help, that the legacy system's schedule returns slots in real time, and that the clinic accepts losing the call where the receptionist usually offers a private exam.

If any of these bets is false, the app goes live and nothing happens. An ASSUMPTION is exactly that: what needs to be true for the solution to work. While it lives in everyone's head and on nobody's paper, it cannot be tested or discussed.

This lesson's work is short and uncomfortable: take each solution you want to build and list, without mercy, everything that needs to be true. Marty Cagan's four risks return here as the four assumption families: value (or desirability), usability, technical feasibility, and business feasibility. Every sentence you write falls into one of them.

And pay attention to empty families. When the list has no business assumption, it is almost never because no risk exists there: it is because nobody on the trio looked at that side.

[["Family","Guiding question","Who usually pulls it"],["Value (desirability)","Do they want it and will they switch from today's way?","PM"],["Usability","Can they use it alone, without help?","Design"],["Technical feasibility","Can we build it on time and at scale?","Engineering"],["Business feasibility","Does it fit cost, legal, support, and brand?","PM with the business"],["All together","What needs to be true for this to work?","The trio in the same room"]]
A solution approved in a meeting is a guess in a tie. Write the bets underneath it and the guess returns to its real size.

## Write it as a testable sentence, not a question

There is a wrong way to list assumptions, and it is the most common one: writing a vague question. 'I wonder whether the manager uses it on mobile?' cannot be tested, because it says nothing about who, how often, and what would count as yes. Always write in the present tense, affirming, with a subject and a number: 'the schedule manager checks the schedule on mobile at least twice a week'. Now you can leave the room and verify.

Three things change when the sentence looks like this. First, the team discovers it disagreed without knowing: one person thought once a month, another thought every day. Second, it becomes obvious whether evidence already exists stored somewhere, like last quarter's mobile access log. Third, the test designs itself almost alone, because the sentence already says what needs to be observed.

A shortcut for reviewing your list: if the assumption cannot be false, it is not an assumption, it is decoration. 'People like convenience' is true in every universe and helps nobody decide anything. Whereas 'the patient swaps the reception's WhatsApp for the app to reschedule' can be false tomorrow morning, and that is exactly why it is worth writing.

## The pre-mortem, or imagine it already failed

When the team gets stuck and cannot list assumptions, the pre-mortem unsticks it in fifteen minutes. The rule of the game: pretend it is already six months from now, the solution launched and failed badly, enough to become a topic at the board meeting. Each person writes alone, in silence, the reasons for the failure. Then you read aloud and group them.

The effect is psychological and it works: talking about an already-consumed failure is socially easier than doubting someone's plan in front of the team. Things come out that nobody would say in a normal meeting, like 'legal blocked sending results by push' or 'the phone database was outdated'.

Each reason that appears becomes an assumption written backwards. 'Nobody found the button' becomes 'the patient finds the reschedule option in under thirty seconds'. 'The integration did not hold' becomes 'the legacy schedule responds in under two seconds at peak time'.

Do this with the whole trio in the room. The PM sees value and business risk first, design sees usability, engineering sees what will break. Alone, you list very well the risks you already knew.

# Not every assumption deserves your time

The trio left the pre-mortem with thirty-two assumptions on the board. Testing all of them would take a semester, and nobody has a semester. The question now is not 'what can we test?', it is 'what needs to be tested before we build anything?'.

The ASSUMPTION MAP solves this with two axes. The first is IMPORTANCE: if this sentence is false, does the solution die or merely get worse? The second is EVIDENCE: how much do we truly already know that it is true? And here the evidence ladder you saw earlier applies, because team opinion does not count as strong evidence, however senior the person.

Crossing the two axes yields four quadrants, and one of them is the one that matters. High importance and low evidence is the project-killing quadrant: these are the sentences supporting the whole solution for which nobody has any proof. That is where you test, now, before writing the first line of code.

The other three quadrants exist so you stop spending energy on them. Important with evidence: document where the proof is and move on. Not important: move on without testing.

The team tests what is easy to test and is then surprised by what was dangerous. Start with the dangerous one.

ASSUMPTION MAP
Solution: app for patients to reschedule appointments on their own
Cycle 12, week 1

   importance: high
   evidence: low (only the sales team's opinion)
   quadrant: project killer, test now

S2 The legacy schedule responds in under 2 seconds at peak
   importance: high
   evidence: low (nobody measured at peak time)
   quadrant: project killer, test now

   importance: high
   evidence: medium (the board said they accept, no number)
   quadrant: project killer, confirm with data

   evidence: low (flow still on paper)
   quadrant: test, but after S1

## How to position without eternal discussion

The most common mistake is not building the map wrong, it is building the map right and testing the wrong thing. The team looks at the dangerous quadrant, sees that testing it takes work, and picks the assumption that is easy to verify. The week ends with a pretty chart about something that decided nothing, while the sentence holding everything up still has no proof.

To position without spending two hours debating, use the silence-first rule. Each person on the trio positions all the assumptions alone, without seeing the others'. Then you compare and discuss only where there was divergence.

Divergence is the exercise's hidden gift. When the PM places a sentence as 'high evidence' and engineering places the same sentence as 'no evidence', the conclusion is almost never that someone is wrong: it is that nobody has real evidence, and what exists is different people's confidence in different sources. A diverging sentence goes straight to the dangerous quadrant.

One final care with the evidence axis. Evidence is what you can show: a number, a recording, a log, a transaction. If the answer to 'how do we know this?' is 'we have always known', the evidence is low.

# The smallest test that produces reliable evidence

You have a dangerous assumption in hand and the team has already started drawing screens. Hold on. The question that opens a test is not 'how do we build this?', it is: what is the SMALLEST thing that produces reliable evidence about this assumption?

Smallest does not mean badly made. It is the test that answers that specific sentence and nothing else. If the assumption is 'the store pays to receive the receivable within 24 hours', you do not need the anticipation engine: you need to know whether the merchant clicks, fills in, and asks to be notified. If the assumption is 'the legacy API responds within two seconds at peak', you need no screen at all: you need two days of spike and a chart.

The anatomy is always the same: the assumption written as a testable sentence, the method, the success criterion agreed BEFORE, the sample size, and the deadline. Five fields, fits on a post-it.

The field almost every team skips is the criterion. 'Let us see what happens' is not a criterion. 'At least 8 of 20 visitors click and leave an email' is. And the difference is not bureaucracy: without a number agreed beforehand, any result becomes 'we found it promising', because the team already invested in the idea and will defend it with whatever appears.
A criterion agreed before is a test. A criterion invented after is a justification with the face of data.

[["Assumption","Cheap method","Success criterion"],["Manager checks schedule on mobile","Look at the mobile access log","Over 40% of accesses on mobile"],["Store pays for anticipation","Landing page with a sign-up button","8 of 20 visits leave an email"],["Legacy returns the schedule in time","2-day spike on the API","Response under 2s at peak"],["New flow explains itself","5 usability tests","4 of 5 finish without help"],["Margin survives free shipping","Spreadsheet with 3 scenarios","Margin above 12% in the worst case"]]

## Cheap method per risk family

Each assumption family has methods that cost little and already deliver signal. Value: conversation with whoever has the pain, demand test with a page and email capture, pre-sale offer. Usability: clickable prototype with five people, or even paper on the table. Technical feasibility: a two-day spike, measuring in the environment that already exists, a conversation with whoever maintains the legacy system. Business feasibility: a margin spreadsheet with three scenarios, a query to legal, a question to support about how many tickets that would generate per month.

Notice almost none of these methods involves building the feature. That is on purpose. Discovery's most expensive anti-pattern is 'let us build it just to test': the team delivers a whole version, spends six weeks, and in the end discovers the value assumption was false. Then nobody has the courage to kill it, because there is already code live and people who defended it at a board meeting.

A one-afternoon test is worth more than a one-month study while the assumption is still coarse. Precision comes later. First you want to know whether you are in the right neighborhood; measuring the lot with a tape measure before that is elegant waste.

## Sample and deadline fit in the week

Two questions stall more teams than they should: how many people and until when. For a qualitative test, five to eight people of the right profile already show the pattern that matters; if the first five conversations point the same way, the sixth rarely turns the game. For a demand test, what matters is having enough traffic for the number to mean something: 20 visitors decide nothing, 300 already say something.

The deadline enters as a project constraint, not an estimate. Instead of asking how long the test will take, agree it ends on Friday and design the test that fits there. That forces the right cut: drop the extra screen, drop the question nobody would use, and what remains answers the assumption.

And write the criterion with the number in front of the team, the same day you design the test. If nobody can agree on a number, that is already information: it means the assumption is still too vague, and the problem is not the test, it is the sentence. Go back to the testable sentence before spending the week.

# Killing the idea cheaply is the goal

Two possible orders for the same set of tests. In the first, the team starts with the clickable prototype, because design had free time; three weeks later, in the user conversation, they discover nobody would trade the current spreadsheet for that. In the second, the team starts with the conversation; by Wednesday of the first week they already know the solution does not hold and return to the opportunity tree.

Same work, completely different cost. The order of tests is a product decision, not a scheduling detail.

The rule is direct: first test the MOST important assumption with the LEAST evidence, the one from the project-killing quadrant. Within it, choose the cheapest method that still gives reliable signal. If two methods answer the same question and one costs two days while the other costs three weeks, start with the two days and only scale up if the result stays ambiguous.

This changes what you celebrate. A test that topples the solution in week 1 is not a team failure: it is the quarter you did not spend building the wrong thing. A mature team logs the money saved and moves on; an insecure team tries to save the idea by fiddling with the criterion after seeing the result.

[["Order","Test","Cost","What it decides"],["1","Conversation with 8 managers","1 week","Whether the pain exists and is worth switching"],["2","Spike on the legacy API","2 days","Whether it can be built now"],["3","Demand page with email","3 days","Whether anyone acts, not just praises"],["4","Prototype with 5 people","1 week","Whether the flow explains itself"]]
When the first test topples the solution, you did not lose the idea: you saved the quarter you would have spent on it.

## Value before usability, technical when it is binary

There is a default order that solves most cases. Value comes before usability because polishing the flow of something nobody wants is perfecting waste. Perfect usability does not save a solution without demand; strong demand survives even a mediocre flow for a while.

The exception lives in technical feasibility. When it is BINARY and expensive, it enters early, sometimes before everything. If the solution depends on data the company does not collect, an integration with a system the vendor will not open, or latency the current infrastructure does not deliver, find that out in week 1. There is no sense validating value for a month to then hear from engineering that no path exists.

Business feasibility follows the same logic: if legal can block it outright, ask before, not after. A twenty-line email to legal is cheaper than any prototype.

The default order, then, is value, technical when binary, usability, and business running in parallel. But the assumption map outranks the default order: if the most dangerous sentence is about usability, start there.

## One at a time, in parallel, and the weekly cycle

Not every test needs to wait for the previous one. The question is simple: does this test's result change the next one's design? If yes, run one at a time. If not, run in parallel and gain a week. The spike on the legacy API and the manager conversations are independent: they can run together, one with engineering, the other with the PM.

The clickable prototype, however, depends on what comes out of the conversations, because a flow designed before understanding the manager's routine tests the wrong screen. That one waits.

Teresa Torres calls CONTINUOUS DISCOVERY the habit of running small rounds every week instead of one giant battery before launch. The practical difference is batch size: three conversations a week, every week, teach more than thirty conversations in March and none until December. And it fits the calendar of people who also need to deliver.

One last rule that saves suffering: stop early. If the first test toppled the assumption holding everything up, do not run the other three just because they were on the spreadsheet. The test plan exists to decide, not to be fulfilled.

# The team's memory against the zombie idea

November. Someone from the board suggests, with great enthusiasm, a cashback program for the app. The PM feels a sense of deja vu, searches three tools and finds nothing. The team tests it again, spends three weeks, and reaches the same bad result as May, when another squad had already tested exactly that. That is the ZOMBIE IDEA: it returns every six months, with the same enthusiasm and the same lack of evidence, because nobody wrote down what was learned.

The learning log is the remedy, and it is much simpler than it seems. For each tested assumption, an entry with six fields: the assumption written as a testable sentence, the test that was done, the date, the observed result in raw numbers, the interpretation, and the DECISION taken.

The field almost everyone forgets is the last one. A log without a decision becomes an archive of curiosities: readable, unusable. With the decision written, the entry answers the question someone will ask eight months from now, which is almost never 'what did you discover?', but 'why did you not do it?'.

LEARNING LOG
Cycle 12, week 3

Assumption
   The patient prefers rescheduling in the app to calling reception

Test
   Page with a 'reschedule in the app' button and email capture
   Sample: 312 visits from the confirmation SMS
   Date: May 12 to 19

Criterion agreed beforehand
   At least 30 emails, i.e., 10% of visits

Observed result
   17 emails in 312 visits (5.4%)
   9 of the 17 wrote 'only if through WhatsApp'

Interpretation
   Interest exists, but below what pays for a whole app
   The channel seems to matter more than the feature

Decision
   Adjust: test rescheduling via WhatsApp link first
   The app assumption stays frozen, not discarded

Owner and review
   Scheduling squad PM, review in 30 days

[["Field","What goes in","Common mistake"],["Assumption","The testable sentence, in the present","Writing a vague question"],["Test and date","Method, sample, and when it ran","Logging only the month"],["Result","The raw number observed","Writing the conclusion already"],["Interpretation","What the number suggests","Mixing it with the raw number"],["Decision","Continue, adjust, or kill","Leaving the field blank"]]
A team without a log repeats the same idea every six months, with the same enthusiasm and the same lack of evidence.

## Where it lives, who reads it, and when to shrink it

The log lives next to the discovery artifact, in the same place as the opportunity tree, and must be searchable by word. One page per cycle, with that cycle's entries, works well. If it is in a document only the PM opens, it is already dead; if it is spread across three tools, it is too.

It has a use nobody anticipates: the log exposes the team's own bias. Read the last twelve entries and count how many times the decision was 'continue' even with weak evidence. If it is almost always, the team is not testing, it is collecting justification for doing what it already wanted to do. That number is uncomfortable and it is the most useful thing the log produces.

The risk on the other side is becoming bureaucracy. A fifteen-field form, a template with a corporate header, nobody reads and everyone fills out by obligation. The rule is honest: if nobody consults it, shrink the format until it fits in five lines.

At bottom, discovery is not a phase that ends nor a calendar ritual. It is the habit of writing what you assumed, what you tested, and what you decided because of it, one round at a time.

lessons.title: The right fidelity for the risk

blocks.value:
# The prototype answers a question

You ask for a prototype to test debt renegotiation in a bank app. Three weeks later a beautiful piece arrives, animated, with polished micro-interactions. The person testing spends the whole session commenting on the button's green, and nobody discovers what mattered: does she understand that this removes her name from the credit protection service?

A prototype is not a pretty mockup. It is a TOOL for answering a question, and fidelity is chosen by the RISK you want to attack. A paper sketch or gray screen serves to test CONCEPT: does the person understand what this is and what it is for? A clickable prototype serves to test FLOW and usability: can she complete the task alone? A prototype with the user's REAL DATA serves to test trust and decision: does she believe the number and act on it?

High fidelity too early is expensive in two ways. It consumes design time you do not yet know is worth it, and it creates attachment, because nobody wants to throw away what came out beautiful. On top of that, it diverts feedback to the button's color. Low fidelity on the wrong test also deceives: nobody decides to trust a bank statement drawn in pencil.

[["Question to answer","Fidelity","Typical time","Trap"],["Understand what this is?","Paper or gray screen","1 to 2 hours","Thinking you tested usability"],["Complete the task alone?","Clickable without final visuals","1 to 2 days","Discussion about color and font"],["Trust the number and act?","User's real data","3 to 5 days","Exposing data without care"],["Worth paying for this?","Real offer page","2 to 3 days","Promising what does not exist"]]
The expensive prototype is not the one that costs money, it is the one you no longer have the courage to throw away.

## Choosing fidelity without falling in love

The practical rule is short: write the question before opening the tool and use the smallest fidelity that answers it. If the doubt is 'do people understand what agreed shipping is?', a poster with three sentences suffices. If the doubt is 'can the merchant configure the shipping rule alone?', you need something clickable, with the real field names. If the doubt is 'does the merchant trust the calculation and turn off their spreadsheet?', their number must appear, with their zip code.

Two signs you raised fidelity too early. The first is the test's agenda becoming aesthetics: the session notes talk more about typography than task. The second is the team defending the prototype when the user gets stuck, instead of taking notes in silence. Attachment is a symptom of high investment.

The reverse path holds too. If the person cannot even understand the concept on paper, no point polishing the clickable: you do not have an interface problem, you have a proposition problem. Raising fidelity at that point only makes the misunderstanding prettier and more expensive to fix later.

# Five people per round suffice

You have budget for fifteen sessions. The temptation is scheduling all fifteen in the same week, running everything, and leaving with a thick report. Do not. Five users per round already catch most of a flow's serious problems, and the sixth person usually repeats what the first five showed. Better to run five, fix what appeared, and run five more on the corrected flow: you spend the same and learn three times as much.

Setting up the session starts with the TASK. A task is a real, specific situation: 'you received a 240-real invoice you do not recognize, resolve it here'. An instruction is not valid. 'Click the top menu and then dispute' delivers the path and measures nothing. If you had to explain where to go, the test ended before it started.

During the session, watch without guiding. When the person gets stuck, count to three before opening your mouth, because silence is where real behavior appears. The two lifesaving questions are 'what are you thinking right now?' and 'what did you expect to happen?'. Neither teaches the path, and both make the person narrate their mental model.

    Finished alone: no, asked for help at minute 3
    Literal quote: 'where is the button to complain about this?'
    Severity: blocking

A usability test answers whether the person can use it. Whether they want to use it is another question, and it does not fall here.

## What the test does not answer

The most common mistake is not in the conducting, it is in the conclusion. The team runs five sessions, everyone completes the task without getting stuck, and someone writes in the report: 'validated, people want it'. They want nothing of the sort. A usability test answers 'can they use it?'. Whether the person WANTS to use it is value risk, and that is discovered another way: an interview about their life, a demand test, money on the table.

You can get both readings in the same session, as long as you separate the notes. On the usability side: where they got stuck, what they expected to happen, how long it took, whether they finished alone, the literal quote. On the value side: whether they asked 'when does this go live?' without you prompting, whether they told a story of needing this, whether they complained about the price. Mixing the two readings produces false confidence.

Close the round with the problem list ordered by severity and repetition. A problem that appeared in four of five participants is a pattern. A problem that appeared in one may be recruiting bad luck, and it is more honest to mark it that way than to turn it into a task on next sprint.

# Measuring demand before building

An auto-parts marketplace decides to launch same-day delivery. Six months of team, integration with three carriers, everything live. First-month adoption: 0.4% of orders. Nobody had asked the market whether that was worth the price, because asking looked less serious than building.

The demand test exists for that: finding out whether anyone wants it, before it becomes code. The methods are few and simple. A LANDING PAGE with a clear proposition and call to action, the classic smoke test. A FALSE BUTTON inside the product, which logs the click and answers 'we are preparing this, want to be notified when it ships?'. A WAITLIST with email. A small ad campaign, to measure how much it costs to bring an interested person. And pre-sale, the hardest test of all.

What separates strong signal from weak is the COST the person pays to signal interest. Clicking costs almost nothing. Leaving an email costs a little, because they know contact will come. Putting in a card costs a lot. It is the evidence ladder applied to demand: opinion at the bottom, behavior in the middle, money at the top.

## Criterion before, ethics always

Before putting up any test, write the number that would make the team continue. Something like: 'if at least 8% of page viewers click, and 25% of those leave an email, we dig deeper; below that, we archive'. Without a criterion written beforehand, any result becomes a defense of the original idea: 40 sign-ups look like a lot to whoever wants to build and little to whoever does not.

Watch the denominator. Three hundred clicks from your loyal client base do not say the same as three hundred clicks from an ad to a cold audience. And watch the test that measures only the ad's quality: a spectacular headline converts well and proves nothing about the product.

The ethical part is not a detail, it is what separates a test from a scam. Never promise what does not exist without warning. Never charge for something you will not deliver; if you charged in a pre-sale and gave up, refund the money fast and explain why. Notify whoever signed up even when the decision is not to build, with a short honest message. And remember the brand pays the bill: a badly run demand test burns the trust of the client you already had.

# People behind the curtain

An accounting startup promises automatic classification of invoices. The client uploads the PDF and, in fifteen minutes, receives the invoice categorized. There is no model at all: there are two analysts on the other side of the screen doing it by hand. In three months, the team discovered forty exception rules that would never appear in a meeting flowchart, and only then started coding.

That is WIZARD OF OZ: from outside it looks automatic, inside there are people doing the work. The user does not know, and that is exactly why the ethical care is greater. Never do it with sensitive data without clear consent, and never with a critical decision without supervision from whoever answers for it: denied credit, medical triage, employee termination.

Its acknowledged cousin is the CONCIERGE. Here the service is declared manual and personalized: the user knows there are people serving them, often talks with that person on WhatsApp, and receives hand-made work. A logistics operation promising route optimization can start with a planner building everything in a spreadsheet and sending it by message, client by client. Both deliver real value before automation exists; the difference is who knows.

If your Wizard of Oz has been running for six months, you do not have a test: you have an operation wearing a software costume.

## When to use each, and when to stop

Choose by what you still do not know. Use WIZARD OF OZ when you need to measure real behavior without bias: if the person knows there are people assembling the answer, they ask differently, wait longer, and forgive errors. Use CONCIERGE when you do not yet understand the process well enough to automate; hiding the human then does not help at all and gets in the way, because the open conversation with the client is half the data.

What you learn in both is the same valuable thing: the exception rules. Anyone can draw the happy path in a meeting. What topples projects is the invoice with the headquarters' tax ID and delivery at a branch, the resume with no end date at the last job, the order changing address after leaving for the route. That only appears when someone does it by hand, a few hundred times.

The limits are clear. It does not scale, it tires the team, and it has an expiration date. Agree beforehand how many weeks it will last and which question ends the test. If it runs half a year, you are no longer testing: you are operating a manual service disguised as a product.

# Producing got cheap, asking stays expensive

In 2026, a product team opens a generative AI tool, describes the screen in two sentences, and receives ten navigable variations in minutes. Another tool generates realistic fake data to populate the prototype. A third transcribes the eight interviews and returns the grouped themes before the coffee cools. The cost of PRODUCING discovery artifacts has plummeted, and that is great.

The side effect is treacherous. It got cheap to produce prototypes and it remains expensive to discover the right question. In practice, the team generates ten beautiful screens on top of an assumption nobody questioned, everyone feels productive, and the error only appears at launch, now with ten screens of emotional investment instead of one.

Separate what the tool accelerates from what it does not replace. It accelerates EXECUTION, VARIATION, and VOLUME: more versions, faster, cheaper. It does not choose which risk to attack, does not recruit the right person, does not listen without leading, and does not decide what to do when the evidence is weak and the deadline is short. Those four remain human work, and they are precisely the ones defining whether the discovery served any purpose.
