The tool generates ten screens in five minutes. It does not generate the question that made drawing one worthwhile.

## The hidden risk in automatic synthesis

The automatic interview summary deserves special attention. The tool transcribes, groups, and returns something like 'users report difficulty in the reconciliation process'. It looks useful, and it is, for finding the excerpt. But the good data almost never lives in the summary: it lives in the literal sentence ('I print the report and check with a pen, because the system already cost me money once') and in the four-second hesitation before answering whether they trust the number.

The summary erases hesitation, erases tone, erases the contradiction between what the person says and what they do. Use the synthesis as an index, not as a conclusion: it points where to listen, and you listen. Keep the literal sentences in the learning log, with participant and minute.

The practical rule that survives any tool fits in one line: write the question and the success criterion BEFORE opening the tool. Done that, use everything that exists to go faster. What changes every year is the cost of producing; what does not change is the discipline of knowing what you are trying to discover and what would make you change your mind.

# A survey does not discover, a survey counts

A delivery-app PM sends a survey to 4 thousand partner merchants with the question 'what is missing in the app?'. Back come 900 free-text answers: 'more promotions', 'faster app', 'lower fee'. Two weeks of work to confirm that merchants want to pay less. The error was not the survey, it was what he asked of it.

A survey is a MEASUREMENT instrument. It answers how many and how often about something you already discovered by talking with people. You interview twelve merchants, three tell the same story of a payout that arrives late and breaks the week's cash. Then the survey enters to say whether that is 6% of the base or 55%. Without the interview first, you write questions about what you imagine and receive back, at scale, exactly what you imagined.

The closed question is where the survey wins or loses. One idea per question: 'is the app fast and easy to use?' has no possible answer for whoever finds it fast and confusing. The user's language, not the team's: if the merchant calls it 'the money that lands', do not ask about receivables settlement. And options covering the whole world without overlapping, always with 'other' and 'does not apply' for whoever does not fit your boxes.

Target time: 6 minutes, 14 questions

## Scale, order, and the time a person endures

Pick ONE scale and use it start to finish. If the questionnaire is agreement from 1 to 5, every opinion question stays 1 to 5, with 1 always as disagree and 5 always as agree. Inverting the direction midway looks clever for catching autopilot responders, but it pollutes the data: many people do not notice the flip and you are left not knowing which answers are misreadings and which are true opinion.

Two biases bring down a good survey. The first is the leading question: 'how much did you like the new screen?' already assumes the person liked it, and she politely goes along. Swap for a neutral wording leaving comfortable room for a bad answer. The second is AQUIESCENCE: there is a human tendency to agree with statements, even more with whoever is providing you a service. It inflates every positive statement in the questionnaire, so distrust when everything comes back 4 and 5.

Order matters. Start easy and concrete, leave the sensitive for later and demographics last, when the person has already invested time and has less reason to leave. And respect the clock: 5 to 8 minutes is the reasonable ceiling. Past that abandonment grows fast, and whoever persists to the end starts marking anything just to finish.

# Ranking ten items produces garbage

An ERP team sends 300 clients a list of ten improvements with the instruction 'drag in order of importance'. Half abandon at the fourth item. Whoever finishes delivers an order that, in a control question at the end, they themselves cannot repeat. The team treats that ranking as truth and prioritizes the whole quarter on top of it.

Ranking ten items is heavy work: it demands comparing each item with all the others, and the brain tires. From the fourth or fifth on, the person orders by guess, a mental tie disguised as decision. The lazy variation is even worse: asking item by item 'how important is this to you?' on a 1-to-5 scale. It costs nothing to say everything matters, so nine of the ten items come back as very important and you are left with a flattened list between 4.1 and 4.6.

The fix is not polishing the instructions, it is changing the mechanics. Priority only appears when there is a TRADE-OFF, when choosing one thing means giving up another. Every good prioritization technique does the same thing: it forces the person to sacrifice something. The two most useful in day-to-day work are MaxDiff and the Kano model, and neither requires advanced statistics to give a useful answer.

## MaxDiff: pick the best and the worst

MaxDiff's idea is simple. Instead of the whole list, you show 4 or 5 items per screen and ask two questions: which of these is MOST important to you and which is LEAST important. The person answers in seconds, because comparing four things is easy. Then you repeat the round with another combination of items, and another, until each item has appeared a few times next to different opponents.

Each such screen carries a lot of information: you learn that group's top and bottom, and by extension that the middle ones lost to the first and beat the last. Adding ten or fifteen quick rounds yields an order with real separation. Instead of ten items squeezed between 4.1 and 4.6, you see what always appears at the top, what nobody ever picks, and the gray band in the middle.

The secret is the forced-choice mechanic. Nobody can say everything is important when the screen demands pointing at the least important one. It fits in an ordinary survey, runs on mobile, and the completion rate usually beats drag-and-drop ordering, because each screen is light.
An importance scale asks what the person wants. MaxDiff asks what they give up. Only the second separates priority from wish.

## Kano: the functional and dysfunctional questions

The Kano model classifies each item with a pair of questions. The FUNCTIONAL one is 'how would you feel if the app opened the statement in one second?'. The DYSFUNCTIONAL one is 'how would you feel if the statement took ten seconds?'. Both use the same five answer options: I like it that way, it is what I expect, whatever, I can live with it, I dislike it. Crossing the two answers classifies the item.

From that comes a direct reading. Basic is what the person expects: nobody praises a working login, but a broken login generates rage and cancellation. Linear is what responds in proportion: the faster the statement, the more satisfied she gets. A Delighter surprises when present, and its absence does not bother, because she did not even know it was possible. And indifferent is what the team finds lovely and the client does not miss.

The practical use is what matters. Basic enters the essential and does not become a sales argument, it only prevents loss. Linear enters the comparison with competitors, it is where the metric moves when you invest. Delighters enter sparingly, one at a time, because they are expensive and age: a good phone camera was once delight and is now basic. Indifferent items leave the list without mercy.

# The product is already telling you things

On an insurance app's dashboard, one number jumps out: 78% of people stop at the document upload step. The team reads that as an answer, concludes the screen is ugly, and spends a quarter redesigning. After launch, 74% stop at the new step. The number was right; the reading was what was wrong.

An abandonment funnel is a QUESTION, not an answer. It says where your base is getting stuck and at what size, and that is extremely valuable information, because it points exactly where the next interview should happen. What it never says is the reason. Maybe the screen is confusing. Maybe the requested document is in a drawer at the parents' house. Maybe the person does not trust sending an ID through an app they met yesterday. Each of these hypotheses calls for a completely different solution, and none of them shows up on the chart.

The discipline is simple to state and hard to keep under pressure: when the data shows a hole, write the question it raises before writing the solution. Five conversations with whoever abandoned cost less than a quarter of redesign and answer what the dashboard cannot.

## Paths, back-and-forth, and internal search

The funnel is only the surface. Underneath it exists the path people actually take, which is almost never the path someone designed in Figma. People who enter through search and ignore the menu, people who go through three help screens before buying, people who leave the app and return through the email link. Comparing the designed flow with the real flow usually yields more opportunity than any brainstorm.

The back-and-forth between screens deserves special attention. Someone alternating three times between the cart and the product page is not strolling, they are looking for information you did not put where it should be: delivery deadline, compatibility, exchange policy. That back-and-forth pattern is one of the most reliable signs of confusion there is.

The cheapest source of all is INTERNAL SEARCH, especially terms that come back with no results. There the user is writing, in their own words, exactly what they came looking for and did not find. If 'second copy of the boleto' appears a thousand times a month in an app that has that feature, the problem is not the feature, it is the path to it. And recurrence is the most honest sign of value: people who come back on their own the following week are saying it solves something.
A funnel answers nothing. It only points, with square-meter precision, where your next interview should happen.

## Caututions and the instrumentation fight

Three traps catch everyone. The first is confusing correlation with cause: whoever uses feature X retains more, but maybe the feature retains nothing and only the already-engaged reach it. The second is forgetting the calendar: a December drop, a post-campaign peak, end-of-month movement in a financial product. Comparing week against week without looking at seasonality produces an invented conclusion.

The third is the most treacherous: aggregate data hides segments with opposite behavior. A stable total conversion may be a steep drop on mobile compensated by a rise on desktop. Before celebrating or panicking over a flat line, break it down by platform, plan, region, and tenure.

And there is the foundation of everything: INSTRUMENTATION. An event without an agreed definition becomes a number nobody trusts. Does order_created fire on the button click or only after payment confirms? If two teams answer differently, the dashboard became a source of discussion instead of a source of truth. The practice that saves is boring and cheap: an event dictionary with name, exact moment it fires, properties, and owner. Without it, nothing else in this lesson holds up.

# The number says where, the interview says why

At an auto-parts marketplace, the dashboard shows that whoever uses search converts four times more than whoever browses by category. The conclusion looks obvious: invest in search. Three interviews later, the story changes. The buyer has no doubt about which part they want, they FEAR the part will not fit their car, and leave the site to confirm compatibility on the seller's WhatsApp. Better search would solve none of that.

Keep that sentence, it organizes the whole module: the number says WHERE and HOW MUCH, the interview says WHY. Each side answers a question the other cannot. The dashboard sees the whole base, but is blind to motive, context, and emotion. The conversation sees motive clearly, but from only a handful of people, and alone you never know whether that handful represents anyone beyond itself.

The team treating the two as rival teams loses twice. The one treating them as a pair of instruments gains something neither delivers alone: a decision with an explained motive and a known size. That is what makes a priority survive the first hard question in a meeting.

## The cycle runs in both directions

The first direction starts at the number. A health app sees that 38% of people who reschedule an appointment in the app call the center within the next ten minutes. No dashboard explains that. Four interviews do: the confirmation screen vanishes quickly, nobody receives a receipt, and the patient calls because they do not trust the reschedule took. The pain was not rescheduling, it was having no proof of rescheduling.

The second direction starts at the conversation. In that same app, four of nine patients tell they write the appointment time on paper on the fridge. That is a beautiful hypothesis, and a hypothesis is not prioritized alone. It goes to the quantitative side to measure: how many export to the calendar, how many open the schedule screen more than three times in the appointment's week, how many take a screenshot. If the behavior appears in 40% of the base, it became a priority with size. If it appears in 3%, it was an interesting detail from four people.

At the parts marketplace, the full cycle would be: the dashboard points to the abandonment, the interview reveals the compatibility fear, a survey measures how many buyers already received a wrong part, and the solution's test returns to the dashboard to see whether the abatement gives. In and out of both sides, always.
A dashboard without interviews optimizes the button that should not exist. An interview without a dashboard scales six people's pain to the whole base.

## The two classic errors and how to present

On one side, generalized quali: six interviews, all pointing at the same annoyance, and someone writes in the document that 'everyone wants this'. Six people are not everyone, and the sentence vanishes from the text the moment you swap in 'six of six people we interviewed said this; we do not yet know the size'. On the other side, context-free quanti: whole quarters spent optimizing a button's click rate when, had anyone asked, that button should not have been on that screen.

TRIANGULATION is the way out of both. When three independent sources point at the same thing, interview, support ticket, and usage funnel, confidence rises much more than when a single source is enormous. The reason is that each source has a different bias, and different biases rarely err in the same direction. A large sample from one channel only repeats the same bias at scale.

For leadership, there is an order that works: the number opens and the user's literal sentence closes. First '31% of merchants had a late payout this quarter', which gives size and credibility. Then 'I failed to pay my supplier because the money did not land', which nobody forgets until the next meeting.

# Do the responders look like the users?

A gym chain sends a satisfaction survey and gets back 72% 'I recommend it'. It goes on the slide, becomes a beaten goal. Except the survey appeared inside the app, for whoever opened the app that week. Whoever canceled was not there. Whoever stopped going in March was not there. That 72% measures the opinion of whoever still uses and still likes it, and the name for that is not base satisfaction, it is satisfaction of the survivors.

The question you ask before looking at any percentage is always the same: do the responders look like the users? Three biases spoil the answer frequently. SELECTION: whoever answers a spontaneous survey is usually the very engaged or the very irritated, and the middle user, who is the majority, stays out in silence. SURVIVORSHIP: whoever canceled left your base, so the list of people you can ask is already cleansed of the worst experiences.

And CHANNEL: a survey inside the app never reaches whoever stopped opening the app, email never reaches whoever does not open email, and a survey at the store register never reaches whoever gave up on the line. The channel picks the sample before you pick anything.

## Size, without heavy statistics

It is possible to be honest without formulas. For a DIRECTIONAL reading of a single segment, a few dozen responses already orient the conversation: if 30 of 40 merchants in a region report payout delays, you do not know the exact number, but you know there is a big problem there worth investigating. Nobody needs a thousand responses to decide whom to talk with next.

But the moment you want to compare two groups or cut by segment, the game changes. Each cut divides the sample, and what is left in each cell becomes noise. Those 40 responses become 12 on the basic plan and 9 on premium, and a seven-point difference between them is indistinguishable from chance. Saying premium is more dissatisfied based on that is inventing.

The hard point is this: a large biased sample is WORSE than a small honest one. The small one you read carefully, knowing it is an indication. The large one gives false confidence, enters the slide with decimal places, and becomes a quarter's decision. Three thousand responses from a single channel do not correct the channel's bias, they repeat the same bias three thousand times.
Seventy-two percent means nothing until you say out of how many. Seventy-two percent of 18 responses is a conversation, not a result.

[["Bias","Who is left out","How to reduce"],["Selection","The average, silent user","Draw invites across the whole base"],["Survivorship","Whoever already canceled the service","Invite ex-clients by email"],["Channel","Whoever stopped opening the app","Use two or three channels together"],["Timing","Whoever only uses at month end","Keep collection open longer"]]

## Reducing bias and reporting properly

Four habits solve most of the problem. Invite through more than one channel, because each channel brings a different slice of the base. Include whoever abandoned: the canceled list is any company's most valuable and least used, and a short email with a single question usually suffices. Compare the responders' profile with the base's profile: if 70% of your clients are on the basic plan and 70% of responses came from premium, you measured premium, not the base. And, when the deviation exists and you cannot correct it, say so in the presentation.

The fourth habit is the cheapest and most ignored: report the DENOMINATOR alongside the percentage. Saying '72% approve' without saying 'out of 18 responses' is deceiving without lying, and sooner or later someone finds out and your whole work loses credit. Write the absolute number, the channel, and the date next to every percentage leaving your hand.

From here on, when someone shows you a research result, your first question is out of how many, and who those people were. It is the table's cheapest question and the one that most prevents a wrong decision.

# 9,400 accounts and almost no rides

Caronae is a fictional corporate carpooling app. The company hires the service, employees sign up, and start sharing cars to and from the office. Whoever drives splits fuel, whoever rides saves on transit, and HR cuts parking and transit-benefit spending. The contract is sold per active employee, with a monthly cost cap per company.

Today's picture: 12 client companies, 9,400 employees with accounts created, and only 11% who completed their first ride within 60 days. One in nine. The rest installed, created a password, looked at the screen, and vanished.

Notice the problem's shape. People entering is not what's missing: HR advertises, sign-up adoption is great, the top numbers look good in any presentation. What does not happen is the second step. This has a name: sign-ups exist, ACTIVATION does not. And activation is what the contract demands, because no company renews paying for idle accounts.

This lesson sets the board for the discovery cycle you will follow to the module's end. Nothing here is too hypothetical: it is the kind of situation that appears in any B2B2C product with easy adoption and hard usage.

[["Candidate goal for the cycle","Type","Works or not"],["Launch the new onboarding in May","Delivery","Measures effort, not outcome"],["Grow account revenue by 20%","Business","Far from what the trio controls"],["Raise activation from 11% to 25%","Behavior","Works: measures what changes in usage"],["Cut parking spending","Business","Consequence, not the trio's lever"]]
Sign-up is promise, a completed ride is proof. Caronae's trio stopped counting promises and went after the proof.

## The cycle's outcome, written in one line

Caronae's product trio (PM, design, and engineering) sat down and wrote the cycle's outcome: raise from 11% to 25% the percentage of employees completing their first ride within 60 days. One sentence, one number, one deadline.

Two alternatives were discarded on the spot. The first was 'launch the new onboarding'. That is delivery, not outcome: the team can launch the most beautiful thing in the world and activation stays put, and the goal is still hit on paper. The second was 'grow revenue'. Revenue is the company's scoreboard, not the trio's lever; between what this team does and billing sit renewal, sales, pricing, and a dozen factors nobody there controls.

The chosen outcome sits in the middle: it describes BEHAVIOR of real people, is measured without creative interpretation, and the trio can move it with its own work. That is the test you apply to any goal offered to you. If it can be beaten by delivering, it is output in disguise. If it can be missed while doing everything right, it is too far from the team.

## What the data tells and what is still guesswork

Before talking with anyone, the trio emptied the dashboard. Usage data shows that 62% of sign-ups open the search screen at least once and leave without requesting anything; that 38% of ride requests end without a driver; that there is one registered driver for every six riders; and that 71% of completed rides happen on the morning route.

That is quite a lot. And it explains nothing. Usage data shows WHERE it gets stuck, never why. On the evidence ladder it sits above opinion and below observed behavior with context, which is precisely what is missing.

The team listed separately what was guesswork: 'people are afraid to ride with strangers', 'the app is confusing', 'drivers are missing', 'people just want to drive alone anyway'. Four sentences said with great conviction in a meeting and zero evidence behind them. Writing the guesswork list is an uncomfortable and absurdly useful exercise: it becomes the agenda of what the interviews need to confirm or knock down.

## Whom the trio will hear, and the cycle's plan

Recruiting by behavior, not opinion. The trio separated three groups: whoever signed up and never rode (the pure blockage), whoever rode once and stopped (lived the whole experience and gave up midway), and whoever became a frequent user. This third group looks dispensable and is the most valuable: the CONTRAST between whoever stayed and whoever left is research's gold, because it shows what needed to go right for the person to continue.

Six conversations, one per day, half an hour each, scheduled directly with HR at the two biggest client companies. No three-month study: it is one week of fieldwork, at continuous discovery's rhythm.

The plan for the rest of this module is the whole cycle, in the order it actually happens. In the next lesson you read real excerpts from the six interviews and watch the synthesis being done. Then, the opportunity tree and the branch choice with explicit criteria. Then, the assumption map and the first two tests. And at the end, the outcome, the decision, and what the team does the following Monday.

# One week of fieldwork, six conversations

Monday through Saturday, half an hour per person, always with two of the trio on the call: one leads, the other takes notes. The rule agreed beforehand was simple and hard to keep: no presenting ideas, no asking 'would you use', no defending the app when criticism appears. Only specific stories, in the past, about the previous week's commute.

It is Rob Fitzpatrick's mom test applied without ceremony: asking questions not even your mother could answer with empty kindness. 'Do you think corporate carpooling is a cool idea?' any polite person answers yes to. 'Tell me how you got home last Wednesday' nobody can embellish.

The excerpts below are cuts from the recordings, the way they stayed in the transcript. Read them paying attention to two things: where the person describes behavior that already happened, and where they hand over a ready solution in place of the pain. Both appear in the same conversation, mixed, and separating them is half the synthesis work.

INTERVIEW 1
Ana, financial analyst, lives 34 km away, daughter in daycare

  Researcher: tell me how your trip home went last Wednesday.
  Ana: I leave at 6:10 pm, take two buses, get home at 7:55 pm.
  Researcher: and on the day you opened Caronae, what happened?
  Ana: I looked for a ride back, two options appeared at 6 pm,
       I stared for a while and closed the app.
  Researcher: what went through your head when you closed it?
  Ana: if the daycare calls and I have to leave at 5, or if my boss
       holds a meeting until 7, the car is gone. Then I'm on the street
       with no plan B. The bus is bad, but the bus is always there.


INTERVIEW 2
Rafael, marketing intern, no car

  Researcher: did you ever take a ride?
  Rafael: in the morning yes, three or four times, it was fine.
  Researcher: and the trip back?
  Rafael: the trip back never worked. I search and there's nobody.
  Researcher: what do you do when there's nobody?
  Rafael: honestly, I don't even search anymore. It became that thing of
       opening, nothing there, opening again, nothing there. It's tiring.


INTERVIEW 3
Marcelo, sales manager, drives every day, own car

  Researcher: you signed up in March and never offered a ride. Why?
  Marcelo: it's my car, you know. It's not fussiness, but it's an hour of
       driving with a person I don't know, having to make conversation.
  Researcher: was there a specific moment that made you give up?
  Marcelo: when the app asked me to confirm my home route. I stopped there.
       I'm not putting my address out for anyone at the company to see.
  Researcher: and if it were someone from your floor, from the sales team?
  Marcelo: that changes it. If I knew who it was beforehand, I'd probably drive them.


INTERVIEW 4
Priscila, service rep, shift schedule changing every week

  Researcher: how do you find out your week's schedule?
  Priscila: it comes out Friday afternoon, and sometimes changes Tuesday.
  Researcher: did you ever book a ride in the app?
  Priscila: I booked one. Then they changed my shift and I had to cancel.
       I was embarrassed to book again and cancel again.


INTERVIEW 5
Beatriz, HR analyst, rode once and stopped

  Researcher: tell me about that one ride you took.
  Beatriz: it was the trip back, booked for 6 pm. At 6:10 the driver canceled
       in the app, without saying anything to me.
  Researcher: and what did you do?
  Beatriz: I went down, ordered a ride-hail car and paid 34 reais.
       That was double what I would save in a whole month.
  Researcher: did you try again after that?
  Beatriz: no. Once is fine, but I won't risk it again.
       If there were a chat in the app to talk to the driver, maybe.


INTERVIEW 6
Diego, developer, uses it four times a week

  Researcher: what made you continue after the first ride?
  Diego: I always ride with Fabio, from the data team. We settled on
       a fixed arrangement: 8 am and 6 pm, Monday to Thursday.
  Researcher: and when one of you can't make it?
  Diego: we say so in the team group in the morning and work it out.
  Researcher: if Fabio left the company tomorrow, would you continue?
  Diego: honestly? I think I'd go back to driving alone.

When the user hands you a ready solution, they handed you the end of the story. Your work is going back and discovering the beginning.

## From loose line to card, from card to branch

The synthesis happened on Friday, with the six transcripts open. The method was the simplest that exists and works: each relevant moment of speech became a CARD, with the literal excerpt written on it. No summary, no interpretation, the person's sentence. 'If the daycare calls and I have to leave at 5, the car is gone' is a card. 'The person fears surprises' is not a card, it is team opinion disguised as data.

Similar cards become a grouping, and the grouping gets a name written IN THE USER'S VOICE. That is how the four names in the table above appeared. Notice none of them mentions screen, button, or feature. An opportunity is a pain, need, or stated desire, period.

Diego's interview, the only frequent user, entered the synthesis as contrast and changed the weight of everything. He is not loyal to the app: he is loyal to Fabio. What sustains his use is a fixed human arrangement, with a plan B settled outside. That reinforced two branches at once: predictability of the trip back and trust in whoever is in the car.

## Pain is not the same as requested solution

Three of the six people asked for a chat in the app. Beatriz asked for it in so many words. It is the classic temptation: half the sample asking for the same thing looks like market consensus, and the team starts building.

The trio did not do that, and it is worth understanding why. Chat is a SOLUTION. It answers to some pain the person could not name, and the work is finding the pain behind it. Beatriz does not want to text with a stranger; she wants to know, before leaving the office, whether the car will be there. Marcelo does not want chat either; he wants to know who will sit in the back seat. The same requested solution hid two different pains, which became different branches.

The practical rule the team adopted: every time someone asks for a feature, the next question is 'tell me about the last time you needed this'. The answer is always a story, and the story is what becomes a card. The requested solution does not die, it just changes place: it goes to the bottom of the tree, as a candidate to be tested later, if its branch gets chosen.

# Caronae's tree on the wall

With the cards grouped, the trio assembled the Opportunity Solution Tree. The structure is always the same: the outcome at the top, opportunities in the middle, candidate solutions at the leaves, and, further down, the assumption tests. It is not a pretty diagram for a status meeting; it is the map of the team's reasoning, and it serves to answer an annoying question that always comes: why are you working on exactly this?

One detail changes everything when assembling: no opportunity enters the tree without a card behind it. If the team wants to hang a branch and cannot find the line supporting it, the branch does not enter. It becomes a question for the next round of interviews.

The four branches below came entirely from the six conversations in the previous lesson. The sub-opportunities are finer cuts of the same theme, because not every big pain gets solved whole at once. And the solutions, note well, always appear in the plural: a single solution hanging on a branch almost always means the team had already decided and went looking for evidence afterwards.

OUTCOME
  Raise from 11% to 25% the employees completing
  their first ride within 60 days

  BRANCH 1: I don't know whether there's a ride for my route before signing up
      sub: I don't want to create an account to find out there's nobody
      sub: my neighborhood never shows up in search results
        solution: preview of active routes without needing login
        solution: email notice when someone from my route appears
        solution: route heatmap sent by HR at onboarding

  BRANCH 2: I don't trust riding with someone I don't know
      sub: I don't know who the person is before accepting
      sub: I don't want to expose my home address to the whole company
        solution: profile with photo, area, and tenure
        solution: public meeting point instead of the address
        solution: ride restricted to the same floor or area

  BRANCH 3: my return time is unpredictable
      sub: if I'm late, the car leaves and I'm left with no plan B
      sub: my shift changes during the week and I can't commit
        solution: return guarantee with ride-hail reimbursement
        solution: flexible window with confirmation up to 30 min before
        solution: pool of on-call drivers from the company itself

  BRANCH 4: I was left stranded when they canceled last minute
      sub: cancellation arrives with no warning and no alternative
      sub: there is no cost at all for whoever cancels
        solution: standby queue triggered on cancellation
        solution: driver reputation visible to everyone

  QUESTIONS WITHOUT CARDS (not branches yet)
      in-app chat: which pain does this truly solve?
      ride gamification: nobody mentioned it, it came from an internal meeting

Choosing a branch hurts because it forces the team to write, in full words, what it will not solve now.

## Four criteria, scores 1 to 3, decision recorded

A tree with four branches is beautiful and paralyzing. The trio agreed on four criteria before scoring, precisely so nobody would score nudging things toward someone's favorite branch. REACH: how many of the 9,400 live this. SEVERITY: how much it blocks the first ride. ALIGNMENT: how much touching it moves 60-day activation. CAPACITY: whether the team can attack it alone, without depending on another area.

The unpredictable-schedule branch won with 12 of 12. Maximum reach because it touches everyone with a variable return time, and the return is exactly where the data shows 38% of requests without a match. Maximum severity because it is the exact point where Ana closed the app. Direct alignment with the first ride. And capacity, because it does not depend on changing contracts or convincing legal.

What stayed out was recorded in writing, with date and reason, in the same document. Trust lost on capacity: touching address exposure and coexistence rules pulls in legal and HR at all 12 companies. Cancellation lost on reach: it hurts a lot for whoever went through it, but there were few cases. Route came close and became next in the queue.

## Three competing solutions for the same branch

Branch chosen, the trio did the part most people skip: it generated COMPETING solutions instead of defending the first idea that appeared. There are three, all attacking the same unpredictable-return pain, and purposely different from one another.

The first is the return guarantee: if the booked ride falls through, Caronae pays ride-hail transportation up to the value of a common trip. It attacks the fear directly, promises a plan B, and requires nobody to change behavior. The second is the flexible window: instead of booking 6 pm, the person books a range between 5:30 and 7 pm and confirms up to 30 minutes before, with a standby driver queue behind it. The third is the on-call pool: the company itself keeps two drivers on standby for the return, paid with a bonus.

The trio chose to investigate the guarantee first, and the reason was honest: it is the one that tests the pain most cleanly. If the plan-B promise unlocks nobody, the other two probably do not either, and the whole branch falls apart before becoming code.

# What needs to be true for the guarantee to work

The chosen solution fits in one sentence: if your ride home falls through, Caronae pays your ride-hail transportation up to a cap. A short sentence, and under it a pile of things the team is crossing fingers to be true without having checked any of them.

This is the moment most teams jump straight to Figma. The trio did the opposite: sat for forty minutes and listed every assumption supporting the guarantee, in Marty Cagan's four risk families. DESIRABILITY (someone wants this), USABILITY (people understand and can use it), TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY (it can be built and operated), and BUSINESS FEASIBILITY (the money closes).

The exercise has one rule that prevents self-deception: write every assumption as a statement that can be FALSE. 'Understand whether people like the guarantee' does not count. 'The fear of being left stranded is the main reason for abandonment, and the reimbursement promise unlocks the first ride' counts. Written that way, you can look at the sentence and ask how much evidence exists behind it. Almost always, the answer is much less than it seemed in the meeting.

ASSUMPTION MAP: return guarantee
If the ride home falls through, Caronae pays ride-hail transportation

  DESIRABILITY
    S1. the fear of being left stranded is what blocks the first ride
        importance: high      evidence: medium (4 of 6 interviews)
    S2. the reimbursement promise is enough for the person to book
        importance: high      evidence: none

  USABILITY
    S3. the person understands the guarantee rule without reading a manual
        importance: medium     evidence: none
    S4. the person can trigger the reimbursement at the moment of distress
        importance: high      evidence: none

  TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY
    S5. the fallen ride can be detected without someone checking by hand
        importance: medium     evidence: medium (the log already exists)
    S6. reimbursement is possible without becoming finance's spreadsheet
        importance: medium     evidence: low

  BUSINESS FEASIBILITY
    S7. the reimbursement cost fits in the company contract's cap
        importance: high      evidence: none
    S8. the guarantee does not become an excuse for drivers to cancel more
        importance: medium     evidence: none

  DANGEROUS QUADRANT (very important, little evidence)
    S2, S4, S7
    attack order: S2, then S7, then S4

## Importance on the upper axis, evidence on the lower

With the eight assumptions on the table, the trio plotted each on a two-axis plane: importance (if this is false, does the whole solution fall?) and evidence (how much we already know today). The upper-left corner, very important and little evidence, is the project-killing quadrant. That is where the team invests testing time, and only there.

Three assumptions fell in that corner. S2, that the reimbursement promise is enough for the person to book: if false, the solution unlocks nothing. S7, that the cost fits in the contract: if false, the solution works and breaks the account. S4, that the person can trigger the reimbursement in the crunch: if false, the promise exists on paper and fails at the moment that matters.

Notice what stayed out and why. S5 and S6 are technical risk with reasonable evidence, because the cancellation log already exists and engineering said outright that reimbursement is a known problem. None of that means S5 and S6 are true; it means testing them first would be spending the week on the wrong risk.

[["Designed test","Risk attacked","Success criterion"],["Guarantee banner, 200 inactive users","Value","15% click and 8% book"],["Concierge at 1 company, 14 days","Business","Average cost up to 12 reais"],["Reading the rule aloud, 5 people","Usability","4 of 5 explain without help"],["Automatic reimbursement spike","Technical","Flow standing in 3 dev days"]]
An important assumption without evidence is hidden debt. Early it costs one week of testing; late it costs a quarter of code.

## The first two tests, with the criterion written before

Test 1 attacks S2 and is ridiculously cheap. HR sends a message to 200 signed-up, inactive employees with the guarantee promise written in one line, and a button to book the week's return. Criterion agreed BEFORE sending: at least 15% click and 8% book. Below that, the team treats it as a weak signal and returns to the tree.

Test 2 attacks S7 and is a classic concierge, what people also call a wizard of oz. At one client company, for two weeks, the guarantee is announced for real and operated by hand: when a ride falls through, the person messages the group, someone from the trio orders the ride-hail car, and finance reimburses outside. No code. What gets measured is how many times the guarantee is triggered and how much each trigger costs.

Why not build the feature to test it? Because the feature would take six weeks of team and answer the same two questions a message and a spreadsheet answer in fifteen days. Building is the most expensive way there is to discover the assumption was false.

# One test passed, the other toppled the solution

Fifteen days later, the two results on the table. The banner test came in well above what was agreed: of the 200 inactive users, 19% clicked and 11% booked a return that same week. The criterion was 15% and 8%. No doubt about what that says: the fear of being left stranded is real, it was indeed blocking people, and the plan-B promise unlocks them.

The concierge told another story. In 14 days, at a company with 61 booked return rides, the guarantee was triggered 23 times. Average cost per trigger: 31 reais. Doing the simple math, that is over 700 reais in two weeks at a single company, against a contract cap that comes nowhere close when you multiply by 12 clients.

The trio's reading was surgical and worth memorizing: the OPPORTUNITY is confirmed, the SOLUTION does not pay for itself. Those are two different conclusions, and confusing them is this step's most expensive mistake. Whoever mixes them throws away the whole branch because of a bad implementation, and returns to zero without needing to.

[["Test","Criterion","Result","Verdict"],["Banner, 200 inactive","15% and 8%","19% and 11%","Passed"],["Concierge, cost","Up to 12 reais","31 reais per time","Failed"],["Concierge, frequency","Up to 15%","23 of 61 rides","Failed"],["Return-time branch","Confirm the pain","Confirmed in both","Kept"]]
A confirmed opportunity with a failed solution is not a failed cycle. It is the cycle working, and charging little for the learning.

## Pivoting the solution without changing the branch

The decision came out of the same meeting: keep the outcome, keep the unpredictable-schedule branch, change the solution. Out goes the return guarantee with reimbursement, in comes the flexible confirmation window up to 30 minutes before, with a standby driver queue behind it.

The reasoning is direct. The pain the banner proved is the uncertainty of getting back. The guarantee attacked that uncertainty by buying a ride, that is, solving it with a variable cost on every trigger. The flexible window attacks the same uncertainty by changing the commitment: instead of promising money when it fails, it lowers the chance of failing. Variable cost near zero, and Diego himself already did this by hand with Fabio, arranging it outside.

The guarantee was not erased from the tree. It became a solution failed on cost, with the number in front, and stays hanging on the same branch. If one day the contract changes shape or cancellation volume drops a lot, it returns to the queue with context. That is the value of keeping the record: next year's team will not spend fifteen days rediscovering what this one discovered.

LEARNING LOG, cycle 07, week 14

  OUTCOME
    60-day activation, from 11% to 25%

  OPPORTUNITY
    my return time is unpredictable

  SOLUTION INVESTIGATED
    return guarantee with ride-hail reimbursement

  HYPOTHESIS (S2)
    the plan-B promise makes the inactive sign-up book
      test: banner to 200 inactive, criterion 15% click and 8% book
      result: 19% click, 11% booking
      reading: confirmed, the pain blocks and the promise unlocks

  HYPOTHESIS (S7)
    the reimbursement cost fits in the contract cap
      test: concierge at 1 company for 14 days, criterion 12 reais
      result: 23 triggers in 61 rides, 31 reais on average
      reading: refuted, variable cost blows the margin

  DECISION
    keep outcome and opportunity, change solution
    in: flexible window with confirmation up to 30 min before
    out: guarantee with reimbursement (failed on cost, not on value)

  NEXT HYPOTHESIS IN THE QUEUE
    the standby queue covers cancellation in under 10 minutes
      planned test: concierge at the same company, 2 weeks

  NEXT WEEK'S INTERVIEWS
    2 with whoever booked through the banner and did not complete the ride
    1 with a driver who canceled a return in the last 30 days

## The cycle does not end, it restarts

The following Monday, no closing meeting. The trio already had three interviews scheduled, the tree gained the note of what was failed, and the next assumption was in the queue, with the test designed. That is the entire point of the continuous discovery Teresa Torres advocates: it is not a study with a final report, it is a weekly habit of contact with whoever uses the product.

Looking at the cycle from behind: a behavior outcome, six interviews in one week, cards becoming opportunities in the user's voice, a tree with four branches, a choice recorded in writing with what stayed out, three competing solutions, an assumption map, two cheap tests with the criterion set beforehand, and a decision that changed the solution without losing the learning. Two and a half weeks. Zero lines of code on the investigated feature.

What you take from this to your work is not the Caronae case. It is the sequence, and above all the discipline of asking, every time someone proposes building something big: what needs to be true for this to work, and what is the cheapest way to find out still this week?
